subject: Vocabulary
topic: Phrasal Verbs II — Meanings and Usage (W11 B2)

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'CALL OFF' as used in: 'The match was called off due to heavy rain.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. CALL OFF = to cancel something that was planned or scheduled. The match was cancelled entirely — not just postponed. Trap: Postponed = delayed to another time (CALL OFF means permanently cancel); Interrupted = stopped midway through (CALL OFF applies before the event starts or completely cancels it). Compare: 'CALL OFF a strike', 'CALL OFF a search', 'CALL OFF a wedding'.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'LOOK INTO' as used in: 'The police will look into the matter.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. LOOK INTO (something) = to investigate or enquire into a matter; to examine something carefully. The police will investigate the matter. Trap: 'Look inside a container' = the literal reading of 'look' + 'into', but as a phrasal verb it means to investigate. Compare: 'We need to look into the cause of the problem'; 'They're looking into the complaint'.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'GIVE IN' as used in: 'After hours of argument, she finally gave in.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. GIVE IN = to stop resisting; to surrender or yield to someone's demands or pressure. After argument, she yielded/conceded. Trap: 'Submitted a document' = 'HAND IN' or 'GIVE IN' (a report/assignment) — this is a different usage where 'give in' is followed by an object. In this sentence, 'give in' is used without an object, meaning to surrender. Distinguish: 'She gave in her homework' (submit) vs 'She gave in' (yielded).

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'PUT OFF' as used in: 'Don't put off till tomorrow what you can do today.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. PUT OFF = to postpone or delay something to a later time. The proverb warns against procrastination — delaying until tomorrow what can be done today. Trap: 'Discourage' = PUT OFF (someone) — another valid meaning of 'put off' (e.g., 'His rudeness put her off'). But in THIS context, 'put off till tomorrow' clearly means to delay/postpone. 'Switch off' = PUT OFF (the light) — yet another meaning. Context determines the right reading.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'STAND BY' as used in: 'He stood by his friend during difficult times.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. STAND BY (someone) = to remain loyal and supportive, especially in difficult times. He remained loyal and supportive to his friend. Trap: 'Stood physically beside' = the literal meaning of 'stand by' (to stand next to something) — but in this context it is clearly figurative (emotional/moral support). 'Waited without doing anything' = to 'stand by' and watch (as in 'standing by' idly — another meaning). Context (during difficult times) confirms emotional loyalty.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'BREAK DOWN' as used in: 'The negotiations broke down after several hours.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. BREAK DOWN = to fail completely; to collapse (used for negotiations, systems, machines, or communication). The negotiations failed completely. Trap: 'Suspended temporarily' = BREAK OFF or ADJOURN (different phrasal verbs); 'Proceeded slowly' = DRAG ON. 'Break down' for a machine = stop working; for a person = have a mental/emotional collapse; for negotiations = fail entirely. All share the sense of total failure or collapse.

questions.stem: Which phrasal verb correctly fills the blank: 'The company decided to _____ the old model and introduce a newer version.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. PHASE OUT = to gradually stop making, using, or providing something (to discontinue gradually). The company is discontinuing the old model. Trap: PHASE IN = the opposite (to gradually start using or introducing something — suitable for the 'newer version'); PHASE OFF and PHASE UP = not standard English phrasal verbs.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'COME ACROSS' as used in: 'I came across an interesting article while browsing the internet.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. COME ACROSS (something) = to find or encounter something by chance, without looking for it deliberately. While browsing, the person unexpectedly found the article. Trap: 'Crossed to the other side' = the literal meaning of 'come across' (to come from one side to another), but as a phrasal verb it means to encounter by chance. Compare: 'I came across an old photograph'; 'She came across as very confident' (another meaning: to appear or seem a certain way).

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'TAKE AFTER' as used in: 'Priya takes after her mother in both looks and temperament.'

options.option_text: Resembles a family member in appearance or character

questions.explanation: C is correct. TAKE AFTER (someone) = to resemble a parent or relative in appearance, character, or behaviour. Priya resembles her mother. Trap: 'Looks after' = LOOK AFTER = to take care of (completely different phrasal verb); 'Runs after' = TAKE AFTER (chase) — a rare alternate meaning, but 'in both looks and temperament' clinches the 'resemble' meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the phrasal verb that means 'to stop doing something that has become a habit':
questions.explanation: C is correct. GIVE UP = to stop doing something, especially a habit or activity that one has done regularly (e.g., 'He gave up smoking', 'She gave up caffeine'). Also means to abandon or surrender. Trap: GIVE IN = to surrender to pressure; GIVE OFF = to emit (give off heat, smoke, a smell); GIVE OUT = to distribute (give out leaflets) or to stop working/run out (the engine gave out). The 'habit' clue points specifically to GIVE UP.
